newsitem.title: GERMANY: GRAF NEED NOT EXPECT "EXORBITANT" SENTENCE--JUDGE.
newsitem.headline: GRAF NEED NOT EXPECT "EXORBITANT" SENTENCE--JUDGE.

text.p: Tennis star Steffi Graf's father need not expect an "exorbitant" jail term if convicted at his tax evasion trial, the presiding judge said on Tuesday.
Peter Graf, 58, has been on trial for two weeks together with a family adviser, accused of evading 19 million marks ($12.57 million) of tax on his daughter's earnings between 1989 and 1993.

Judge Joachim Plass told the court he had ordered Graf to be released from detention for the rest of the trial because, after serving 13 months in investigative custody, "any remaining sentence would not be exorbitantly long".
This suggested that Graf, if convicted, would get a sentence substantially below the maximum 10-year penalty for tax evasion.

Plass last week agreed to release Graf on bail of three million marks, but he remains in detention for now while a higher court considers an appeal by prosecutors who want him to stay in prison, fearing he might flee the country.
Peter Graf submitted a personal declaration to the court pledging to report to police twice a week and do nothing to endanger the course of the trial, such as giving interviews.
Steffi Graf remains under investigation, although she says she left her financial affairs to her father from an early age.
She told a newspaper last week that prosecutors were waiting for the outcome of her father's trial to decide whether to drop the investigation against her in return for payment of a fine.

Peter Graf maintains tax authorities signalled their approval of his schemes to reduce tax on his daughter's earnings by channelling the money abroad, rather than see Steffi join an exodus of German sporting tax exiles.

Documents presented to the court on Tuesday indicated that federal tax authorities in Bonn knew in 1987 of Peter Graf's companies in the Netherlands and the tax haven of the Netherlands Antilles, but did not know Graf was behind them.
A memorandum from the finance ministry in Peter Graf's home state of Baden-Wuerttemberg said Graf had gone there in early 1987 to broadly float the idea of channelling money abroad.
The document included the remark: "We told Mr Graf to make sure he found good advisers for this."
